title: Nvidia halts H200 chip shipments to China after $2.4 billion quarter, leaving 600,000 processors stranded in Hong Kong
summary: Nvidia has stopped shipping its licensed Hopper AI chips to China, interim chief executive Colette Kress said on the company's earnings call, ending a controversial export arrangement just one quarter after it generated $2.4 billion in sales. Around 600,000 H200 processors now sit in storage in Hong Kong, with no clear path into mainland China.
content:
Nvidia has stopped shipping its most powerful artificial intelligence chips to China, closing the door on an export arrangement that lasted barely a year and generated $2.4 billion in a single quarter.

Interim chief executive Colette Kress confirmed the halt on the company's earnings call on Tuesday, November 17. "Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she told analysts, according to Reuters. She gave no reason for the decision and did not say whether it is permanent.

The Hopper family includes the H200, a processor used to train and run advanced AI models and manufactured for Nvidia in Taiwan by TSMC. The chips were only allowed into China under a special licensing arrangement negotiated by former chief executive Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump. Mr Trump approved the exports in December 2025 under strict conditions, and the US Commerce Department began reviewing applications case by case in January 2026. But by February, not a single chip had been delivered because of a slow approvals process, and the sales that eventually flowed were modest by Nvidia's standards: the $2.4 billion booked in the quarter ended October 25 amounted to roughly 2.2 percent of the company's $107.6 billion in data centre revenue for the period.

What happens next to the hardware already built is now the most pressing question. Reuters reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were being stored in Hong Kong, awaiting permission to enter mainland China after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. Neither Nvidia nor the Chinese authorities have said what will happen to that stockpile, whether the chips will be redirected to other markets, returned, or simply left in warehouses while the two governments negotiate.

The halt also exposes how quickly the politics around the chips have shifted. Mr Huang resigned last week after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with the head of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China. On the same day as the earnings call, Nvidia's board created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to handle the company's dealings with US government agencies, and board chairman Harvey Jones told analysts the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

A second, less noticed rule may matter more to Nvidia in the long run. On November 16, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security tightened the rules on how Chinese companies can rent computing power abroad. Until now, export controls stopped advanced chips from being shipped to China, but a Chinese company could still rent computing power on those chips from a data centre in another country. Under the new rule, a data centre anywhere in the world needs a licence before it receives advanced US chips if it gives Chinese companies or other restricted buyers large amounts of computing power remotely. Data centres already serving those customers have 90 days to apply, and chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil now need licences too. Ms Kress said Nvidia still needs time to study the new rules before judging their impact.

Beijing, for its part, has been pulling in the opposite direction. Chinese regulators have restricted H200 imports and encouraged domestic technology companies to buy home-grown processors instead, as part of a broader push to cut reliance on American technology. That leaves Chinese AI firms caught between two governments: Washington will not let the chips in through the front door or the back, and Beijing is reluctant to let them in at all.

The commercial damage to Nvidia looks limited, at least for now. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion and guided the current quarter to $130 billion, plus or minus 3 percent, with no data centre revenue from China included at all. In other words, the world's most valuable chipmaker has written its second-biggest market out of its forecasts entirely, and its guidance still points to growth. Investors have noticed the wider chill: [global technology stocks have slid as the AI rally has faltered](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026), and rival chipmaker AMD has come under pressure of its own after a short seller alleged a blacklisted Chinese firm was using its firmware, as [Global Wire reported this week](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/amd-shares-fall-hunterbrook-china-firmware-report-november-2026).

The timing adds a diplomatic edge. The announcement came as Mr Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, with technology controls high on the agenda. For all the talk of a thaw between the two leaders, the H200 halt shows that the chip war is moving in only one direction: tighter. The question now is whether the 600,000 processors in Hong Kong become a bargaining chip in those talks, or a monument to a deal that collapsed before it really began. [BusinessWorld has the full account of the halt and the licensing arrangement behind it](https://bworldonline.com/technology/2026/11/18/794712/nvidia-stops-shipping-us-approved-ai-chips-to-china/).
